extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, and readers interested in constitutional design and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for structuring constitutions so as to preserve liberty and avoid tyranny, emphasizing mixed government, separation of powers, and institutional safeguards. Draws on historical examples (England, Sparta, Rome, Carthage) and philosophical authorities (Swift, Franklin, Polybius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative, executive, and judicial powers are carefully separated from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim/near-verbatim authority: "the legislative, executive, and judicial powers are carefully separated from each other." Explanation: separation prevents concentration of power; cited as present in the United States and contrasted with other governments. Examples: England (balanced by other mechanisms), United States (carefully separated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government / balance of one, few, and many
rubrics_metrics.description: Power should be balanced among the one, the few, and the many (a mixed government), so no single order holds absolute control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing and justification: "power in the last resort, was always placed by them in balance, among the one, the few, and the many... a mixed government... is by no means of Gothic invention, but hath place in nature and reason." Historical models: Sparta (reges, seniores, et populus), Rome, Carthage, Polybius' three-form government. Danger: breaking the balance leads to tyranny (examples: Rome's subversion under Caesar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances enforced by a third 'hand'
rubrics_metrics.description: A balance presupposes a third hand or institution that can remove or add power to keep the scales even; balance cannot be maintained between only two orders without a third to aid the weakest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor and mechanism: "The balance may be held by the weakener, who by his address, removing from either scale, and adding his own, may keep the scales duly poled." Examples: Decemviri, Ephori, the four hundred, the thirty; Franklin/wagoner analogy used to illustrate why more than one assembly or power-check is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: A people preserves its power by constantly refusing a standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a concrete institutional safeguard: "constantly refusing a standing army." Example: England preserved power of the people by preferring legislative share at expense of a standing army. Implicit rationale: standing armies enable executive/military dominance, threaten liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials by jury should be preserved in their full form and glory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit normative claim: "trials by jury are preserved in all their glory." Presented as part of the suite of liberties that sustain a free constitution (alongside habeas corpus and free press).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus in force
rubrics_metrics.description: The writ of habeas corpus should remain in full force as a protection against arbitrary detention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed with other fundamental protections: "the habeas corpus is in full force." Signaled as essential to the rule of law and personal liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free press
rubrics_metrics.description: A free press is an essential institutional element of a free state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: "the press is the most free in the world." Presented as part of the constellation of liberties that enable laws to govern and public opinion to check power.

rubrics_metrics.name: No hereditary titles or legal distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no hereditary titles, honours, offices, or distinctions that create artificial inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit normative rule: "there are no hereditary titles, honours, offices, or distinctions." Rationale: prevents entrenched privileged classes and preserves civic equality of right (though not equality of natural qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty of the people and popular representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereignty should reside with the people; property and political power should be in the hands of citizens with representatives (senators, governors) chosen regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "Our people are undoubtedly sovereign — all the landed and other property is in the hands of the citizens — not only their representatives, but their senators and governors, are annually chosen." Emphasizes regular, popular election (annual elections cited), popular control over offices, and civic ownership of property as foundations for republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent, ascertained limits of power for each party
rubrics_metrics.description: The limits of power deposited with each party ought to be ascertained and generally known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original quote: "the limits of power deposited with each party, ought to be ascertained and generally known : the defect of this is the cause of... struggles in a state." Guidance: transparency and clear constitutional allocation reduce conflicts and encroachments between orders (few, many, one).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators must account for social inequalities (wealth, birth, family influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must recognize and manage natural and acquired inequalities — wealth, birth, family spirit — because they influence political power and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's list of inequalities: 1) inequality of wealth; 2) birth (family reputation, ancestry); plus family spirit that perpetuates office-holding. Guidance: legislators cannot assume literal equality of citizens' capacities; institutions should be shaped acknowledging these realities to prevent corruption, faction, or undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against popular-assembly excesses and majority tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular assemblies can be subject to the same vices as individuals (cruelty, revenge, sophistry) and may become tyrannical; do not assume many hands are inherently safer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual claims: "it is an error to think it an uncontroulable maxim, that power is always safer lodged in many hands than in one... they are as capable of enslaving the nation." Examples and warnings: popular assemblies can be duped, can exalt single leaders, and when balance breaks may lead to despotism (examples: Carthage, Rome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional openness and merit-based officeholding
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices should be equally open to competition; individuals must take pains and behave well to deserve and hold office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: "While every office is equally open to every competitor... some men must take more pains to deserve and acquire an office than others, and must behave better in it, or they will not hold it." Guidance emphasizes merit, competition, and conduct standards for officeholders to maintain republican virtue and prevent hereditary or family entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant vigilance and corrective mechanisms to preserve constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no constitution is immortal, careful management, vigilance, and corrective measures can preserve a strong constitution and prevent degeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor and passage: likening a state to a body whose humours must be balanced; "we may manage a sickly constitution, and preserve a strong one; we may watch, and prevent accidents; we may turn off a great blow from without, and purge away an ill humour that is lurking within." Guidance: provision for remedial institutions and practices to address internal and external threats.
